name: Sara Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We don't work for employers, AI companies, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell or campaign. This is confidential, so you can separate what you'd say publicly from what you think privately. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Sara, forty-three, and I wire houses and repair the electrics in small shops. I've got a vocational certificate and an electrician's licence, and enough years doing this that I can handle the ordinary faults without someone looking over my shoulder. I like a careful repair that lasts; what wears me down is getting a new phone form when the old paper one worked.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is home like at the moment?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Milan works in payroll, and we have two children, nine and twelve, and a mortgage. My pay is low for this trade, we've got about eighteen days of expenses saved, and there are only a few other electrical firms nearby. I don't use AI tools at all; I keep fault notes in a little blue book and prefer someone showing me a change in person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a steady trade is worth more than another meeting about machines. If the office saves a little time, I'd want the crew to get a proper lunch break out of it. I'd bring that up at our union meeting instead of pretending a faster form is a pay rise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm already anxious about money. Milan and I can pay the mortgage while both wages arrive, but a fortnight of lost pay would leave a very short bridge to the next bill. My licence proves I can do electrical work; it doesn't make the small firm pay more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my repair and wiring shifts now and through the first year, using the same paper notes. I'd go to the union meeting next month and ask for protected lunch breaks and the pay review we've been promised. At home we'd stop the weekly café breakfast and put the money towards ordinary bills, not call it a new savings pot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though relieved not to have another huge thing to learn. A good repair makes sense to me; the balance after the mortgage payment still makes me wince.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you bring to the union meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The last month's late finishes written in my diary, with the days we ate in the van. I want a clear request about time and pay, not a meeting where everybody nods and nothing gets written down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the café cut solve the budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, it's a small weekly amount, not a second wage. It stops us spending money we need for bills while we wait for a real pay decision.

say: I'd say a **steady trade** matters more than another meeting about machines.
I'd ask the union to turn **small time savings** into proper lunch breaks rather than pretend forms are a pay rise.
think: I'm already **anxious about money**, because both wages are needed for the mortgage.
My **licence and experience** do not make the low-paying firm offer more, and our reserve covers eighteen days.
do: Keep **repair and wiring shifts** and the same paper notes now and through the first year.
Attend next month's **union meeting** to request protected lunch breaks and the promised pay review.
Stop the **weekly café breakfast** and use the money for current bills.
feel: **Anxious about bills**, while relieved not to face another major system to learn.
S0.quote: My licence proves I can do electrical work; it doesn't make the small firm pay more.
fieldNote: Her **licence and experience** support ordinary independent repairs, but low pay and few employers leave the household exposed despite practical competence.
She keeps **paper habits** and seeks collective time and pay terms, while the café cut covers bills rather than new savings.

steps.text: Keep the repair and wiring shifts using paper fault notes
Ask the union for protected lunch breaks and the promised pay review
Stop weekly café breakfasts to help cover current bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say do not call it progress until the people losing hours have a paid way into other work. I'd ask the union to press both employers about training and written notice before cuts. The office staff are part of a working family too, not just a cost somebody found a way to erase.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect Milan's payroll hours to be cut sharply when the checking and answering work moves to software. My repairs should continue, but my low wage can't cover the mortgage, food and both children alone. I'm already lying awake over the prospect of opening a pay slip with half the number we depend on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now we'd write down essential bills against my wage and ask Milan's employer for its staffing plans in writing. I'd take that budget to the union adviser next month and ask what support or paid training places actually exist, without assuming we qualify. In the first year I'd keep my repair shifts and cancel the planned new kitchen cupboard doors before ordering them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, and cross when people tell us to enjoy the time saved. Time saved for a firm isn't the same as money left in my kitchen drawer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the union adviser need to tell you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Which help is a grant, which is a loan and what proof of reduced hours each one needs. I don't want to fill the gap in our budget with a payment we only imagined we would receive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your own work in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The physical repairs still need doing, though faster booking may put more visits in the day. I'd keep doing them and keep my safety checks, rather than claim every task vanishes because the office changes.

say: I'd ask for **paid routes** into other work before celebrating the loss of people's hours.
I'd want the union to seek **written notice** and training terms from both employers.
think: I expect **sharp payroll-hour cuts** for Milan as routine checking and answering move to software.
My **low repair wage** cannot cover the mortgage and both children alone, despite physical work continuing.
do: Write an **essential-bills budget** against my wage and request Milan's employer's written staffing plans.
Ask the **union adviser** next month about real support, eligibility and paid training places.
Keep **repair shifts** and cancel uncommitted cupboard-door spending during the first year.
feel: **Alarmed and sleepless** about losing a large part of household income, despite keeping her own practical work.
S1.quote: Time saved for a firm isn't the same as money left in my kitchen drawer.
fieldNote: Her **household alarm** comes through expected payroll-hour losses, not an assumption that thinking software instantly performs hands-on electrical repairs.
She asks for **real eligibility terms** before counting support, and protects the current repair wage while cutting an order not yet placed.

steps.text: Ask the union adviser about support eligibility and actual paid training places
Keep the home and shop repair shifts
Cancel the planned cupboard-door purchase before ordering

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking work goes in 2028 and physical robots follow around 2031, so families need help at both points. I'd want the union in the room before people are asked to sign away hours. A promise to teach me something later won't pay a mortgage this winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most of Milan's payroll income to go in 2028, before I can earn enough extra to replace it. Then robots around 2031 could reduce my own repair hours, and I'd be forty-eight with children still depending on us. Eighteen days saved isn't enough to wait calmly for two employers to find us a future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd call the lender with Milan and ask what temporary mortgage options exist, including interest and the total debt afterwards. We'd ask my sister what emergency childcare she can genuinely offer if one of us gets a paid interview or course place. In the first year after 2028 I'd apply for advertised repair posts only where the written wage and guaranteed hours improve the budget after travel, keeping this job until an offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but I can make the calls with Milan sitting beside me. The household numbers still don't add up. I wouldn't describe a list of phone numbers as a funded answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask your sister for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Specific afternoons, not a promise that she'll somehow manage whenever we need her. My sister has her own job, and I won't tell Milan childcare is settled before she has agreed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take an unpaid course if it looked promising?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not while it meant missing the wage for food and the mortgage. I'd need the fee paid and my normal wage kept before I could consider it, however hopeful the advertisement sounded.

say: I'd ask for help at **both dates**, thinking work in 2028 and physical robots around 2031.
I'd want the union involved before workers sign **reduced-hours agreements** or accept vague training promises.
think: I expect **most payroll income** to go in 2028 before my wage can replace it.
Robots could later cut **my repair hours**, leaving an eighteen-day reserve against a mortgage and dependent children.
do: Ask the lender now for **mortgage options**, including interest and the total debt afterwards.
Ask my sister about **specific childcare afternoons** before treating emergency help as agreed.
Apply after 2028 for **advertised repair work** only with guaranteed hours and written pay improving the budget after travel.
feel: **Alarmed**, able to make calls with her partner but without a funded household solution yet.
S2.quote: I wouldn't describe a list of phone numbers as a funded answer.
fieldNote: Her **two-stage exposure** separates the partner's expected 2028 wage loss from possible later reductions in physical electrical work around 2031.
Mortgage options and **childcare help** are enquiries, while another job requires an actual vacancy, signed terms and a better household budget.

steps.text: Ask the lender about mortgage options, interest and total debt
Agree specific emergency childcare afternoons with my sister if she can help
Apply after 2028 for posted repair jobs with guaranteed hours and pay improving budget after travel
Keep current job until a suitable offer is signed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to build paid apprenticeships for adults as well as school leavers. I'd help the union ask employers for actual places, with the wage and teaching hours written down. People shouldn't have to spend their rent money proving they are willing to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both wages could shrink, but five years gives us longer to prepare than the quick picture. I could investigate equipment-servicing classes before planning changes in 2031; robots follow around 2034, when I'll be fifty-one. I don't suddenly like new technology, and I won't assume any course makes either of us safe forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd attend the union's monthly training meetings now and ask for a small in-person servicing class with the same instructor. I'd enrol after 2031 only if the employer pays the fee, keeps my normal wage and gives a written description of the supervised paid tasks afterwards. Milan and I would review the bills quarterly and try saving thirty monthly only after every essential bill is covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less pinned down by the calendar. I can imagine learning with a person beside a workbench much more easily than being sent home to master a new screen alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ask for the same instructor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I learn slowly when every button changes and I don't want to start explaining that from scratch each week. A familiar person can show me the difficult part again without making a performance out of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course covers fees but not wages?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then it doesn't fit our budget. I'd keep doing repairs while the union asks for a paid route rather than sign up and hope the grocery bill disappears.

say: I'd ask for **paid adult apprenticeships**, not only places for school leavers.
I'd want the union to obtain written **wages** and teaching hours before families commit rent money.
think: Both **wages could shrink**, but five years gives us longer to prepare before planning changes in 2031.
I can learn **different equipment slowly** without assuming a course protects either of us from later robots.
do: Attend **monthly union meetings** now to seek a small in-person servicing class with a familiar instructor.
Enrol after 2031 only with **employer-paid fees**, maintained normal wages, the same instructor and a written supervised paid-task description.
Review bills **quarterly** and save thirty monthly only after essentials are covered.
feel: **Anxious but less cornered**, able to imagine repeated practical instruction at a workbench.
S3.quote: People shouldn't have to spend their rent money proving they are willing to learn.
fieldNote: Her **resistant habits** persist: she wants repeated in-person instruction rather than becoming an AI user simply because she has longer to prepare.
The **thirty-monthly saving** depends on essential bills, while training explicitly covers wages as well as tuition and describes actual paid work.

steps.text: Attend monthly union meetings to seek paid practical adult training places
Enrol after 2031 only with employer-paid fees, maintained wages and supervised paid tasks described in writing
Save thirty monthly only after essential bills are paid
Choose small in-person servicing only with the same instructor each week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the children should see a range of work, not be told there is one safe path because their mother fixes wires. I'd ask the school about free work visits and let them choose where they want to look. I'd still support the union asking for paid adult learning before it becomes an emergency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The long warning helps, but low pay and eighteen days saved still worry me now. Thinking AI arrives in 2036, when I'll be fifty-three, and robots around 2039, when I'll be fifty-six. The children will be nineteen and twenty-two in 2036, but I can't assume they need no help or that the mortgage has vanished.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the monthly union meetings and the conditional thirty saving plan now. This year I'd ask the school for free visits across several kinds of work for the children. In the first year after 2036 I'd take the small in-person servicing class only with paid fees, my normal wage kept and actual supervised paid tasks named beforehand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about this year's money, though less frightened by the distant timetable. I could let the children talk about what interests them without checking every interest against a forecast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the children contribute to the mortgage by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, and I wouldn't write that into the plan. They may be studying, earning little or living elsewhere. My children's future wages aren't money sitting in our account now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would more warning change your use of AI today?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I still don't use it, and I wouldn't pretend to be keen because the interviewer gave me ten years. I'd ask for a person to show me what my actual job requires when it changes.

say: I'd support **varied school work visits** rather than tell the children my trade is the only safe route.
I'd want **paid adult learning** arranged before the future change becomes an emergency.
think: Our low pay and **short reserve** worry me now even with a decade of warning.
I cannot assume **older children** need no help or that our mortgage is gone when robots arrive around 2039.
do: Continue **union training meetings** and save thirty monthly only when essential bills allow.
Ask the school about **free work visits** in fields the children choose.
Take **in-person servicing** after 2036 only with employer-paid fees, maintained wages, the same instructor and named supervised paid tasks.
feel: **Anxious about current bills**, but less frightened by the distant change and more open to ordinary family conversations.
S4.quote: My children's future wages aren't money sitting in our account now.
fieldNote: She **ages the children** consistently without assuming their possible adult income pays the mortgage or removes every family expense.
Her **training conditions** and non-use of AI remain intact; more warning changes the urgency rather than rewriting her habits or resources.

steps.text: Continue monthly union meetings to seek paid adult training places
Save thirty monthly only when essential bills allow
Ask the school for free work visits across fields the children choose
Take in-person servicing after 2036 only with employer-paid fees, maintained wages and named supervised paid tasks

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I expect Milan's pay to go before our household has any way to replace it. Paid practical training with our wages kept would help, and clear temporary support if the income falls. I'd want the union checking the written terms so someone learning slowly isn't left agreeing alone.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether a family has enough money for the time everyone says it has. Three years between thinking AI and robots is not three years of free food. A person can have time on a calendar and no room in the weekly budget.

headlineQuote: A person can have time on a calendar and no room in the weekly budget.
portrait: Sara is a **43-year-old licensed electrician** with a vocational certificate and ordinary repair experience, earning lower pay despite her competence.
She has **eighteen days saved**, few nearby employers, a mortgage and two schoolchildren with payroll-working partner Milan.
She **never uses AI**, trusts paper fault notes and wants repeated instruction with a familiar person before learning unfamiliar equipment.
She is **anxious before AI**, alarmed by expected payroll-income cuts, and seeks union-backed paid training with explicit household funding conditions.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove Milan's payroll income before the household can replace it.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid practical training** must preserve wages as well as cover fees.
**Clear temporary support** and union scrutiny of written terms would help if income falls.
